title: Build and publish a DX-CAD plugin | DX-CAD by Designmatix

headings.t: Build and publish a DX-CAD plugin
6. Say which plugin API it needs

text:
Build and publish a DX-CAD plugin
Designmatix Ltd. Last updated 13 November 2026. For DX-CAD 0.1.6, plugin API 7.
In short. Write a Python module with a register(registry) function, declare it as a dxcad.plugins entry point, check it with dxcad-sdk check, build it as a wheel (.whl) and publish the file. DX-CAD users install it from Help > Add-ons > Install from File. The SDK is free and open source under the Apache License 2.0; see the SDK page.
What you need
Start from the template
Write the plugin
Check it and try it
Test it
Say which plugin API it needs
Build the wheel
Publish it
How users install it
A paid plugin
Where to read more
1. What you need
Python 3.12 (DX-CAD runs on 3.12 only, not 3.13), and DX-CAD and the SDK installed together in a virtual environment of their own, so your plugin can be loaded and run while you work on it:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate (Windows; on macOS or Linux: source .venv/bin/activate)
python -m pip install dxcad dxcad-sdk
dxcad doctor
dxcad doctor ends with SMOKE OK when DX-CAD works, and its plugins line names the plugin API this DX-CAD has.
2. Start from the template
The SDK's source, on GitHub at github.com/faizaldm/DX-CAD-SDK, has a starter in template/ and three worked examples in examples/ (a washer, a spacer and a part counter). Copy template/ to a folder of your own, say my-plugin, and rename dxcad_myplugin in both places: the module's file name and its entry in pyproject.toml. The template's pyproject.toml declares the plugin:
[project]
name = "dxcad-myplugin"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A DX-CAD plugin"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
[project.entry-points."dxcad.plugins"]
myplugin = "dxcad_myplugin:register"
[tool.setuptools]
py-modules = ["dxcad_myplugin"]
The entry point's name, myplugin here, is the plugin's name: its menu and its toolbar in DX-CAD's window carry it.
3. Write the plugin
DX-CAD calls your register function once as it starts, handing it the registry. Each call on the registry adds one thing: a name for model.py, a dxcad subcommand, a tool for AI agents, or a command in the window.
def plate(width, depth, thickness):
"""A plain plate, its corner at the origin."""
from dxcad.model import make_box
return make_box(width, depth, thickness)
def add_plate(window):
document = window.document
document.add(document.unique_name("plate"), plate(100.0, 60.0, 3.0))
def register(registry):
registry.require(2)
registry.add_name("plate", plate)
registry.action("add_plate", "Add Plate", add_plate)
With it installed, a model.py can say part("plate", plate(80, 40, 2)), and the window has a menu and a toolbar holding Add Plate. Two rules keep a plugin working everywhere:
Take from DX-CAD only dxcad.model and dxcad.plugins, and import them inside the functions that use them, as above, so the checker can load your module without DX-CAD.
The installed DX-CAD (the Windows installer, the macOS app, the Linux AppImage) runs your plugin in its own Python. There you may import the Python standard library (but not tkinter), any OCP (OpenCASCADE) module, and the PySide6 modules QtCore, QtGui, QtWidgets, QtSvg, QtSvgWidgets, QtNetwork, QtPrintSupport, QtOpenGL, QtOpenGLWidgets and QtPdf. Anything else must travel inside your wheel. The SDK's README has the full list.
The registry can also add model.py names, subcommands (registry.command), tools for agents (registry.tool), kinds of sheet-metal part, and views, annotations and tools for drawings. The plugins page lists every call.
4. Check it and try it
dxcad-sdk check my-plugin
python -m pip install -e my-plugin
dxcad plugins
dxcad gui
dxcad-sdk check checks the plugin's declarations before DX-CAD loads it, one line per check. Installed with -e, your folder is used as it is, so each change shows the next time DX-CAD starts. dxcad plugins lists what each plugin registered, or why one was skipped. dxcad gui opens the window with your plugin loaded.
5. Test it
Tests of a plugin call the real DX-CAD, which keeps its settings, licence, log and recovery files in the user's own folders. Copy the template's tests/conftest.py into your tests/ folder: it sets DXCAD_HOME to a folder of each test's own, so your tests never touch the settings of the DX-CAD you use every day. Then:
python -m pytest
dxcad-sdk sweep myplugin
dxcad-sdk sweep NAME opens each of your window commands offscreen and checks its dialogs fit a 1366 x 768 screen at 100, 125 and 150 percent, that OK, Cancel, Esc and Enter work, and that every part it adds is a valid solid. Before you publish, install your wheel (step 7) into an installed DX-CAD as a user would (step 9) and run its doctor --addons (dxcad.exe doctor --addons on Windows): it imports every installed add-on's modules in the installed DX-CAD's own Python and names each that fails.
6. Say which plugin API it needs
Each DX-CAD has a plugin API version: DX-CAD 0.1.6 has plugin API 7. Your register calls registry.require(N) with the version it was written for: the lower that number, the older the DX-CADs it loads in (the plugins page says which version brought each call), and the [project] table of your pyproject.toml says the same with a classifier, which DX-CAD reads before it installs your wheel:
classifiers = ["Framework :: DX-CAD :: Plugin API :: 2"]
DX-CAD refuses, with the reason, a wheel built for a later plugin API than it has, so a user is told before anything is installed. A wheel without the classifier is taken as built for API 1; registry.require still checks when it loads.
7. Build the wheel
python -m pip wheel --no-deps -w dist my-plugin
This writes one file, such as dist/dxcad_myplugin-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl. A plugin written only in Python gives one py3-none-any wheel that installs on Windows, macOS and Linux alike. A plugin with compiled modules needs a wheel for each platform, built on that platform: win_amd64, macosx_..._arm64 for Apple silicon, and manylinux_..._x86_64. DX-CAD refuses a wheel built for another platform, with the reason.
Raise the version in pyproject.toml for each release: DX-CAD shows it in Help > Add-ons, and installing a newer wheel replaces the older one.
8. Publish it
Publishing a plugin is putting its .whl file where your users can download it:
a release on GitHub (or any code host) with the wheel attached;
a download link on your own website;
or PyPI, for users who run DX-CAD from Python with pip. PyPI accepts only the classifiers on its own list, so leave the DX-CAD classifier out of a wheel you upload there; DX-CAD then takes it as built for API 1, and registry.require still checks the version when it loads.
Say on your download page which DX-CAD versions and platforms the plugin is for, and give your plugin a licence of your own: the SDK's Apache License 2.0 lets you choose any licence for a plugin you write with it.
9. How users install it
Download the plugin's .whl file.
In DX-CAD, choose Help > Add-ons..., then Install from File..., and pick the file. DX-CAD checks it is a DX-CAD plugin for this platform and plugin API before it installs anything.
Restart DX-CAD. The plugin's menu and toolbar are there, and Help > Add-ons lists it with its version, publisher and licence state, where it can be disabled, enabled or removed.
From a terminal, dxcad addons install FILE.whl does the same. DX-CAD installs add-ons into its own add-ons folder, never into the installed program, so this works with the Windows installer, the macOS app and the AppImage alike.
10. A paid plugin
A plugin can say it needs an entitlement with registry.require_entitlement(name, link). Until an installed entitlement provider (an entry point in the dxcad.entitlements group, whose holds(name) answers True or False) says it is held, the plugin loads locked: its menu and toolbar show, greyed, with the words "Requires NAME: see LINK", where the link is your buy page. How you sell the plugin and grant the entitlement is up to you. The plugins page gives the details.
11. Where to read more
The plugins page: every registry call, a minimal plugin, testing, and building against DX-CAD in CI.
The SDK on GitHub: the template, the examples and the source of dxcad-sdk.

text:
DX-CAD › Sheet metal
Sheet metal in DX-CAD
Sheet metal design software with flat patterns ready for the laser
Draw the part in 3D, bend it the way your press brake will, and send the laser or plasma table a flat pattern worked out from how the part was made, not guessed back from the solid.
Download the 30-day free trial See pricing
A sheet-metal tray with corner relief and two holes, modelled in DX-CAD
Everything a sheet part needs
Flanges, returns and hems
Start from a base flange of any outline, then add flanges on its edges at any angle, with returns, open, closed or teardrop hems, and your own bend radius per flange.
Corners and relief
Corner treatments where two flanges meet, with the gap you choose, and bend relief so the corners form cleanly.
Holes, cutouts and slots
Round holes, rectangular cutouts and rounded slots at any angle, through the base or a flange, placed where they will be on the flat.
Materials and mass
Mild steel, stainless 304, aluminium 5052 and galvanised steel, each with its density, so every part shows its mass.
Flat patterns you can cut from
K-factor, or DIN 6935
Give each sheet its thickness, inside bend radius and K-factor, or let DX-CAD take the K-factor DIN 6935 gives for that radius and thickness.
Gauge tables, and your own
The common metric gauges from 0.7 to 6 mm ship for each metal. Keep your shop's own table as a CSV, with your radii and K-factors, and DX-CAD uses it instead.
DXF for your CAM
The flat pattern exports as DXF with the outline on one layer and one line per bend on another, arcs kept as arcs. Shop export profiles give the layers the names your CAM expects.
Checked, not hoped
Flat lengths are checked against hand calculations in DX-CAD's own test suite, run on every change before a release.
From sketch to flat in four steps
Draw the base outline, or pick a gauge and type its sizes.
Add flanges, returns and hems on its edges, and holes or slots where you need them.
Unfold it: DX-CAD works out the flat pattern, with its bend lines.
Export the flat as DXF for the laser, and the part to a drawing for the brake.
Or as a short script
Every sheet part is also a few lines of Python, so a family of brackets is one script with its sizes at the top.
spec = SheetSpec.from_gauge("mild steel", 2)
tray = base_flange([(0, 0), (200, 0), (200, 120), (0, 120)], spec)
for edge in range(4):
tray = flange(tray, edge, 30)
part("tray", tray, color="steel")
Questions
Which K-factor does DX-CAD use?
The one you give the sheet. If you would rather not choose, din_k_factor gives the value DIN 6935 sets for that inside radius and thickness, and the shipped gauge tables use it.
Can I use my own gauge and bend table?
Yes. Keep a CSV of material, thickness, bend radius and K-factor; DX-CAD uses your values for the metals it lists, and refuses a thickness it has not got, naming the nearest.
What does the laser or plasma table get?
A DXF of the flat pattern: the outline and every hole, cutout and slot as lines and arcs, and the bend lines on a layer of their own. Export profiles rename the layers to suit your CAM.
Does it do cones, transitions and elbows?
Those are developed surfaces, made by the Fabrication add-on, which is unlocked during the free trial.
How much does it cost?
Every install is free for 30 days, with every feature. After that a DX-CAD licence is £249 per user per year, plus VAT where it applies.

title: Your first part in ten minutes: a bracket with four holes | DX-CAD by Designmatix

headings.t: Your first part in ten minutes

text:
Examples
Your first part in ten minutes
From installing DX-CAD to a bracket with four holes, exported as a STEP file. The bracket is one of the examples that ships with DX-CAD: a short script with its numbers at the top.
1. Install DX-CAD
Windows: an installer, or a portable zip that needs no Python; both carry dxcad.exe, the command line.
macOS (Apple silicon) and Linux (x64) builds.
Or, with Python:
pip install dxcad
dxcad doctor tells you the install works, ending with SMOKE OK, and dxcad doctor --report gives everything a bug report needs.
Free for 30 days from first start, then a licence. Opening, viewing and exporting stay free. Download DX-CAD.
2. Get the bracket
Copy the example out, then open it in the window:
dxcad examples bracket
dxcad gui bracket.py
The window shows the model in a pane on the right, and the part it builds on the left.
3. Read the numbers
The model is a script, bracket.py, and these are its numbers, at the top of the file:
LENGTH = 80.0
DEPTH = 30.0
HEIGHT = 46.0
THICKNESS = 6.0
HOLES = 4
HOLE_DIAMETER = 5.0
INSET = 10.0
The bracket is an L in section, drawn once and extruded along its length. Every other size follows from these names.
4. Run it
In the window, choose Model > Run Script, or press F5. The same model builds from the command line into a project, and one more command says in words what was built:
dxcad run bracket.py --output bracket.dxcprt
dxcad describe bracket.dxcprt
It is one valid solid, 80 x 30 x 46, with a volume of 33128.761: the L's area times its length, less four holes.
5. Four holes from one line
The script makes one drill, a cylinder through the base, and repeats it in a row. The holes are spaced from the length, so they move when the length does:
pitch = (LENGTH - 2 * INSET) / (HOLES - 1)
drill = make_cylinder(HOLE_DIAMETER / 2, THICKNESS, origin=(INSET, (DEPTH - THICKNESS) / 2, 0))
drills = linear_pattern(drill, (pitch, 0, 0), HOLES)
part("bracket", cut_all(body, drills), color="steel")
Counting them, the part has four holes, each of diameter 5 and depth 6, with centres at x = 10, 30, 50 and 70, y = 12.
6. Change a number
Change LENGTH = 80.0 to LENGTH = 100.0 in the pane and run it again with F5. The bracket is now 100 x 30 x 46 with a volume of 41528.761, and the four holes are at x = 10, 36.667, 63.333 and 90. That is the whole of DX-CAD's parametric model: change a number and run it again.
7. Export it as STEP
Choose File > Export Parts..., pick STEP as the file type and give it a name. It writes the picked parts, or every part when none is picked, to one file; the command line writes them the same way with dxcad export.
Save the project, with its model, with File > Save.
